banner.headline: Your brand is a bit outdated and needs a new image?
banner.body: Tell us about your project and what you want to achieve.

narrativeSections.heading: Context
paragraphs: ContextIn 1928, ten clubs founded La Liga. CE Europa was one of them. A century later, football became an industry. Sponsors replaced supporters. Stadiums became stages. CE Europa stayed in Gràcia. Same postcode since 1907. Three thousand members, four thousand seats, a neighbourhood that still walks to the match. The club had the history and the people. What it didn't have was an identity that looked like either.

narrativeSections.heading: Insight
paragraphs: Postcode pride. Not nostalgia, not heritage. CE Europa is a street club with the elegance of a historic one. We held both sides. A system loose enough to feel like a sticker on a lamppost, structured enough to carry a hundred-year-old crest. Football clubs chase the screen. CE Europa didn't need to. Adapting was a way to keep the status, not to ask for it.

narrativeSections.heading: Idea
paragraphs: The crest came first. We stripped what was redundant, kept what was the club. Cleaner proportions, built for digital. A clear direction from the presidence: ‘Change the minimum.’ The Escapulat, core of the club, became the spine. While Murri Studio typography sets the structure and becomes a key element of the brand the custom software turns the stripes into waves, becoming passion and celebration rendered as pattern.

narrativeSections.heading: Application
paragraphs: From the crest to the shirt, from the app to the stickers that will end up on every bar in Gràcia. The generative tool isn't a backdrop. It's the club's voice as image, a different wave for every match, every goal, every season.

narrativeSections.heading: Impact
paragraphs: A club that founded La Liga, returning to Gràcia with the identity it always had on the street, now on the crest too. Back to Gràcia. New identity. Same postcode.

narrativeSections.heading: Context
paragraphs: ContextEvery February 2nd, the world looks to a burrow. At DDB, they seized Groundhog Day to launch an activation for the new Audi Q3 — and decided that day would never be the same again. This year, the groundhog left its burrow… to stay in a Q3.

narrativeSections.heading: Application
paragraphs: The social media activation was built around 4 animated pieces telling the story of the groundhog and its love affair with the Q3, along with a series of static pieces bringing to life a contest with a prize to match: an experience with the new Q3.

narrativeSections.heading: Impact
paragraphs: 1.7M impressions, 18k interactions and 794 new followers.
And something harder to measure: proving that production-company-level work can be done on a timeline and budget that only make sense for social.

banner.headline: Your brand is a bit outdated and needs a new image?
banner.body: Tell us about your project and what you want to achieve.

narrativeSections.heading: Context
paragraphs: Europe consumes around 3.5 million croissants a day. Chocovic has supplied them for 150 years. Not the chocolate you photograph. The chocolate that gets baked at four in the morning, dropped into buns, melted into glazes. A working product in a category obsessed with looking premium. The brand had drifted there too — cleaner, glossier, further from the bench. The work was to bring it back to where the chocolate actually lives: in the hands of the baker, before sunrise.

narrativeSections.heading: Insight
paragraphs: Chocolate at Heart was the strategic territory, defined by Hamlet. The design had to translate it. We took the idea somewhere else. Made to be used. Heart as the centre of the working chocolate. The thing in the middle of the croissant, the bun, the glaze. A utilitarian identity for a brand that exists to be opened, scooped, melted, baked. Not admired.

narrativeSections.heading: Idea
paragraphs: Made to be used. The system was built from inside the bakery, not outside it. We designed in VR building every element by hand. A utilitarian uppercase wordmark, a block of letters made to be read. Warm and wide, the palette stretches across every product and surface. Photography goes warm and dirty: real places, real hands, dough on the bench. The brand exists at arm's length from the chocolate. Always.

narrativeSections.heading: Application
paragraphs: The system lives in the bakery, not on the screen. The packaging is built to be seen from across the room — large formats, high contrast, the 3D chocolate textures scaling up into colour blocks visible through flour and steam. The website carries the system online, but the bench is where the brand is read. From two metres away, before anyone has touched it.

narrativeSections.heading: Impact
paragraphs: Chocovic now speaks the language of the bakers it serves. The packaging is read from across the obrador. The system holds across every product family, every market, every surface, without thinning out.

narrativeSections.heading: Context
paragraphs: ContextIn the summer of 2025, Audi introduced its new hybrid range with a spot that framed the technology as if it had come from another planet. It ended on a wink: a toy alien. That detail became the most talked-about part of the campaign on social. Audi and DDB decided to turn it into an activation — 30 units of the figure, given away among the community — and brought us in to produce it.

narrativeSections.heading: Application
paragraphs: ApplicationThe campaign kicked off with a full-3D reveal piece, steeped in nineties sci-fi aesthetics — a tone that hooked people and left them waiting for what came next. Then came the mechanics piece, where the alien comes to life, followed by a rollout across multiple posts to keep the pulse going on social throughout the activation.

narrativeSections.heading: Impact
paragraphs: 1.2M interactions. 4.9K comments. 1.3K giveaway entries.
And a project that until recently wouldn't have been feasible on this budget or this timeline: feature-animation finish, at the speed and cost of a campaign that only lives on social.

banner.headline: Your brand is a bit outdated and needs a new image?
banner.body: Tell us about your project and what you want to achieve.

narrativeSections.heading: Context
paragraphs: ContextDiari Sport has covered FC Barcelona and Spanish sport from Barcelona since 1979. Forty-six years of print authority now read on a phone, in the gaps between everything else. The rebrand had to carry a legacy masthead into a feed-first landscape without thinning either side.

narrativeSections.heading: Insight
paragraphs: Youth with heritage. Not a balance — both, at full volume. The knowledge of a paper that has watched every Barça era pass through its pages, and the speed of a publication competing with the timeline. We held the tension instead of resolving it. Sport stays a newspaper. It just stops looking like one from 1979.

narrativeSections.heading: Idea
paragraphs: The wordmark carries the idea in its smallest unit: inktraps. Borrowed from print, where they exist to keep type legible at small sizes, here they become the system. They open and close depending on size and device — sharp on a headline, soft on a favicon. Heritage in the gesture, freshness in the behaviour. Around the wordmark, a design stripped of decoration: bolder, clearer, lighter. A newspaper that reads like a magazine.

narrativeSections.heading: Application
paragraphs: Built with Wete, the system runs across the daily edition, the digital product, social, and editorial covers. Every asset is engineered for an in-house team producing at the speed of sport — templates that hold the brand without needing a designer in the room. The inktraps scale from a stadium-sized cover to a 16-pixel app icon, and the wordmark behaves the same way in both. The system does the heavy lifting.

narrativeSections.heading: Impact
paragraphs: 30% audience growth since the rebrand. Sport now ranks among the four most-read sports outlets in Spain. Hamlet set the direction. Wete built the engineering. The Sport editorial team carried the rollout with the kind of internal conviction that turns a rebrand into a daily practice. Youth with heritage, holding both sides, printed and posted with the same voice.

banner.headline: Do you have a great idea and it needs a brand story?
banner.body: Tell us about your project and what you want to achieve.

narrativeSections.heading: Context
paragraphs: Living longer only matters if you live better — that is Yaba's motto. The category had turned cold, individualistic and American: biohackers tracking every metric, beige brands selling mindfulness, supplements promising twenty more years. The challenge was to step away from all of it. Not a product brand, but a house of six wellness brands distributing across the Mediterranean.

narrativeSections.heading: Insight
paragraphs: An operational contradiction. Yaba is a holding company with M&A, global supply chain and investment banking behind it. But it speaks to someone buying collagen on a Tuesday morning. We put selection at the centre. The rigour of a curator, the warmth of the South. Corporate where it needs to be, human where it matters. Mediterranean balance — the idea, and the operating principle.

narrativeSections.heading: Idea
paragraphs: A Mediterranean attitude towards life, deeply inspired by the work of Joan Miró — colourful, joyful, eternal. The wordmark holds its centre. Longevity runs clinical. Life runs warm.

narrativeSections.heading: Application
paragraphs: Born from the idea of an eternal calm, the corporate site lets every brand sit without competing — NaturaleBio, Aethern, PureChimp, Incite, MDNA, NBio. The system scales without breaking. Each brand keeps its voice; Yaba holds the frame. They don't sell brands. They introduce them.

narrativeSections.heading: Impact
paragraphs: Twelve countries. Six brands in the ecosystem and a business that has doubled in two years. The real credit goes to the Yaba team, who held the balance with a strategic clarity rarely found in a group growing this fast. That's what turns a house of brands into a movement. Living longer, lived better.
[Quote from Patxi or Alex — one line, naming the transformation, not the work.]

title: The Seam
tagline: Fit to Care. Designed to Last.

banner.headline: Do you have a great idea and it needs a brand story?
banner.body: Tell us about your project and what you want to achieve.

narrativeSections.heading: Context
paragraphs: 13 million garments are thrown away in the UK every week. Shein drops up to 10,000 new styles a day. For years the conversation around fashion had been stuck between buying or tossing. Repair existed — the third way — but split between the impersonal local dry cleaner and the unreachable Savile Row, neither of them right. The Seam was born to fill that gap, a platform connecting customers and local makers, from sneakers to Chanel.

narrativeSections.heading: Insight
paragraphs: Caring for clothes had to feel aspirational for the high-fashion buyer, without losing the circular economy at the core of the business. The category went one way — earthy, ethical, a little worthy. But care isn't a value reserved for the conscious shopper. A grandmother cares. A Savile Row tailor cares. Care works the same from Chanel to Carhartt. It's a matter of craft, not attitude.

narrativeSections.heading: Idea
paragraphs: We put the maker at the centre. Fit to Care held both sides — premium without being cold, human without being nostalgic. Seaming became the verb: to sew, to join, the gesture of the craft turned into a system. The S of the wordmark is two figures meeting. The typography cuts sharp, like needles. Deep lilacs over dark backgrounds — cold where the category goes earthy and beige. A circular brand that spoke about its makers, not about itself.

narrativeSections.heading: Application
paragraphs: From the app to collaborations with Adidas and Net-a-Porter, the system applies to every touchpoint. The platform is product — the app is the brand in operation. Art direction warms the cold palette back up: makers in their studio, no flash, no posing. And inside every order, a label that doesn't thank you for buying. It thanks the customer for caring, signed by the maker who did the work. A printed message, a name written by hand. From the first message to the garment returned home.

narrativeSections.heading: Impact
paragraphs: From 500 to 400,000 Instagram followers after the rebrand. Collaborations with Adidas and Net-a-Porter. The brand carried the weight without losing the craft. The real credit goes to The Seam's team, who held the consistency with a discipline rarely seen. That's what turns a system into a living brand.
Layla — CEO & Founder, The Seam

narrativeSections.heading: Context
paragraphs: ContextThe Champions Burger travels across Spain in search of the country's best burger. On June 9th, 2026, it landed at its biggest stop yet: Camp de Mestalla. Over 300,000 people in a stadium built for finals. Through Laia&Laura, we were commissioned to create the teaser that would open the event.

narrativeSections.heading: Application
paragraphs: A spot with Super Bowl soul: stadium epic, hyper slow motion and food porn in equal parts. The burger isn't introduced — it's crowned. Tight shots, ingredient by ingredient, with the level of detail a product this mouthwatering demands.

narrativeSections.heading: Impact
paragraphs: 1.2M views, 600 interactions and 300,000 attendees waiting at Mestalla. Super Bowl finish on timings that are anything but. And not a single burger wasted in the process.

banner.headline: Do you have a great idea and it needs a brand story?
banner.body: Tell us about your project and what you want to achieve.

narrativeSections.heading: Context
paragraphs: White bottles, blue accents, clinical sans-serifs, a stock photo of a smiling pharmacist. Incite had forty-plus SKUs across vitamins, minerals, sports, mood, and herbals — and the existing system made them indistinguishable from a Boots own-label. The brief was simple to say and hard to do: keep the science, lose the pharmacy. The customer was already active, already informed. The brand wasn't catching up to them.

narrativeSections.heading: Insight
paragraphs: We treated the range as a wardrobe, not a pharmacy. One brand, many moods. The lever was colour, because colour is the one signal a pharmacy will never use confidently. Supplements made simple — Incite's own line — kept the promise of clarity. We just changed what clarity looked like. Sporty, not sterile. Made for the gym bag, not the medicine cabinet.

narrativeSections.heading: Idea
paragraphs: No clinical blue and no warning red. Sorbet pinks, court greens, citrus yellows. The chromatic register of sportswear and energy drinks, not of medicine. Typography sits between editorial and athletic: a clean grotesk for product names, weighted heavier than the category expects. Photography keeps product flat, lit hard, shot against its own colour. Every bottle reads as its own object. The range reads as one family by rhythm, not by uniform.

narrativeSections.heading: Application
paragraphs: The system applies at every scale. A quiz-led navigation lets the customer enter by goal, not by ingredient. The smallest move is the label itself: name, dose, benefit, nothing else. No "advanced complex." No "premium formula." The white space on the bottle is the loudest thing in the category

narrativeSections.heading: Impact
paragraphs: Forty-plus SKUs unified under one system, sold direct across the UK and through Yaba's European network. The brand kept the trust of an active customer base — ultra-runners, weekly sport players, the people the supplement aisle wasn't built for — and gave them something worth being seen with.
